newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN boss - no to "another Gaza or Israel in Bosnia".
newsitem.headline: UN boss - no to "another Gaza or Israel in Bosnia".

text.p: The U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday urged the international community to stay in Bosnia long enough to help keep the federation together and not to allow it to become another Gaza or Israel.

"We have a job to do -- the international community, that is. I hope we'd have the patience and the determination to sustain the effort. I think it is essential that we help Bosnia stay together," he told a news conference in Geneva.
Annan, formerly head of peacekeeping at the United Nations, said the international community was obliged to help Bosnia to avoid the creation of a Greater Serbia or Greater Croatia.

"If Bosnia falls apart, then you may have a Greater Serbia or Greater Croatia. What would become of that little strip pf land in the middle? Would it be a Gaza or would it be an Israel? Can we afford to have another Gaza or another Israel?"
Former Yugoslavia's disintegration touched off ethnic war among Serbs, Croats and Moslems in Bosnia.

The U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord ended 43 months of war in 1995. But more than a year later, only 250,000 of the 2.1 million uprooted Bosnians have returned home despite the right to return being central to the peace treaty.
Most are blocked from returning by the failure of the international community to push separatist leaders, mainly in Serb and Croat areas, to stop ethnic intolerance and harassment.
Annan, the first black African and the first U.N. insider to hold the post of secretary-general, said the world needed to have a longer-term presence in former Yugoslavia.

"What we are there to do in Bosnia needs time and will take time. Those on the ground who are doing it now should stay to repair its infrastructure, really manage the reconstruction," he said. "Our world should take a longer-term view of things."
He defended the U.N.'s actions in former Yugoslavia and in the Bosnian Moslem enclave of Srebrenica, where some 7,000 Moslems were massacred while under United Nations protection.
"Because the U.N. went in and obliged all the big powers to work under U.N. umbrella, it prevented them from getting involved individually and competitively with disastrous results," he said.
"The massacre of Srebrenica was a collective defeat, a defeat for all of the international communuity," said Annan.
He said the Security Council had not given the U.N. the necessary means needed to defend the Moslem enclave.
